name: The Atonement: Nature, Extent, and Necessity

objectives.text: Identify that Jesus died on the cross to take away sin
Name Jesus as the Lamb of God and repeat John the Baptist's words about Him
Recall that Jesus took the punishment for sin that we deserved
Retell the Passover story and describe how the blood of the lamb points to Jesus
Summarize substitution as Christ dying in the place of sinners
Describe what the Bible teaches about the shedding of blood for the forgiveness of sins
Explain propitiation as Christ's sacrifice turning away God's righteous wrath against sin
Describe the Day of Atonement ritual and explain how Hebrews presents Christ as its fulfillment
Compare the repeated Old Testament sacrifices with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice
Explain reconciliation as the restoration of peace between God and sinners through the cross
Explain redemption as Christ paying a ransom to set His people free from sin and the curse of the law
Explain from Scripture how Christ's finished work is the ground of the believer's assurance of forgiveness
Analyze why, according to Scripture and the Reformed confessions, God could not simply overlook sin without satisfaction of His justice
Explain why no sinner or mere creature could make satisfaction for sin and why the Mediator had to suffer as true man and true God
Interpret Isaiah's Suffering Servant song in context as a prophecy of penal substitution
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects Christ's active and passive obedience to the justification of sinners
Distinguish expiation, the removal of sin's guilt, from propitiation, the turning away of God's wrath
Analyze the Gospel accounts of Gethsemane and the cry of dereliction to explain how Christ bore God's wrath in body and soul
Explain Christ's triumph over sin, death, and the devil as a biblical aspect of the cross grounded in His satisfaction for sin
Explain the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement from texts that describe Christ dying for His sheep, His church, and those the Father gave Him
Analyze universal-sounding atonement texts in their context and explain the Canons of Dort distinction between the sufficiency and efficiency of Christ's death
Explain how the Reformed tradition holds together definite atonement and the free offer of the gospel to all people
Construct a reasoned defense of definite atonement that interacts fairly with Arminian and hypothetical universalist views
Trace the historical development of atonement doctrine from the early church through Anselm, Abelard, and the Reformers
Evaluate the ransom-to-Satan, moral influence, and governmental theories against the biblical case for penal substitution
Evaluate modern objections that penal substitution portrays divine violence by examining the Trinitarian unity and willingness displayed at the cross
Compose a theological synthesis showing how the cross satisfies divine justice and displays divine love

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (sin taken away, Lamb of God, punishment borne, substitution, propitiation, Old Testament sacrifices compared, assurance, necessity, Isaiah 53, active and passive obedience, definite atonement defense, rival theories, justice and love). Replaced the vague blood observation with a Scripture-grounded objective on blood and forgiveness. Turned the assurance objective into an explanation of the scriptural ground rather than an experience. Separated expiation and reconciliation into distinct objectives and added redemption, Passover, Day of Atonement, the necessity of a divine-human Mediator, Gethsemane and the cry of dereliction, Christ's victory over the powers, exegesis of universal texts with Dort's sufficiency and efficiency distinction, the free offer of the gospel, historical development, and modern objections. Removed whole-chapter citations and attached confessions only where they state the doctrine, adding Heidelberg Q1, Q12-17, Q37, Q44, Shorter Catechism Q25, Belgic 21, and specific Canons of Dort Head 2 articles.
